articles.author: Vildanden
articles.description:
If you keep pasting the branch diff and "write a PR title and body, then wait" into Claude Code, turn that prompt into a slash command. The file name becomes the command; $ARGUMENTS lets you name the base branch or add extra instructions.
Save this as .claude/commands/pr.md:
---
description: "Draft a GitHub pull request from the current branch"
argument-hint: "[base branch | extra instructions]"
---

Draft a GitHub pull request for the current branch. Do not create it until I confirm.

1. Run `git status -sb`, `git log --oneline -15`, and `git diff origin/HEAD...HEAD` (or `main...HEAD` if `origin/HEAD` is missing). If there is no unique commit versus the base, stop and say so.
2. If I passed arguments (`$ARGUMENTS`), treat the first token as a base branch when it looks like one (`main`, `master`, `develop`, or `origin/...`). Treat the rest as extra instructions.
3. Propose a PR title and a body with a short summary, a test plan, and any follow-ups. Do not add AI attribution unless I ask.
4. Show the title and body and wait for me to confirm before running `gh pr create`. Never force-push, never merge, and never add reviewers I did not name.

Use it as /pr, /pr main, or /pr develop include a migration note.
Slash commands are markdown files in .claude/commands. Claude Code injects the file as the prompt and replaces $ARGUMENTS with whatever you type after the command. Keeping "wait for confirm" and "never force-push or merge" in the command reduces unattended PR creation.
Pair this with an "ask" permission rule for gh pr create if you also want a permissions bump.
Commit the command file so every teammate gets the same workflow.
Pair with a /commit command so the branch messages and the PR body stay consistent.
I keep copy-ready Claude Code configs (CLAUDE.md templates, slash commands, hooks, permission rules) in Vildanden Agent Config. There's a free sample: https://justly-mia-429.rehost.page/
articles.title: Draft a GitHub pull request in Claude Code with a /pr slash command

Summary: Page size is one of the most important storage decisions in GBase Database(GBase 8s). It is configured when a dbspace is created and cannot be changed afterward. This guide explains how to configure page size, choose the right value for your workload, understand its relationship with BUFFERPOOL, and avoid costly storage migrations.
Page size is one of the few database storage parameters that cannot be adjusted after a dbspace has been created.
In GBase Database(GBase 8s), the default page size is 2KB, with four supported options:
2KB
4KB
8KB
16KB
The maximum supported page size is 16KB, and each option is a multiple of 2KB.
You specify the page size during dbspace creation using the -k parameter of onspaces.
For example:
touch /data/gbase/datachk01
chown gbasedbt:gbasedbt /data/gb…
articles.title: GBase Database Page Size: Why 2KB to 16KB Must Be Decided Before Creation

A daily report is not a cron-expression problem. It is a delivery contract: start the work once, tell many subscribers about the same shipment state, and make a retry harmless. For a healthtech system, that contract matters more than shaving a few lines from the scheduler configuration.
Short answer: schedule a public Node.js webhook to enqueue the report, keep the webhook short, and let a worker send email tasks idempotently. Treat the scheduler as a trigger, not as the place where the report is rendered. This design fits a daily email report when the work can be handed off quickly; a workflow engine is a better boundary for long-running dependencies or joins.
Infrai fits the trigger-and-handoff slice when one REST interface and one key reduce integration friction across backend services.…

articles.description:
AI coding assistants can generate an Android screen, connect an API, and produce a working APK surprisingly quickly.
But a working APK is not the same as a secure application.
Consider a delivery platform. A driver opens the app, sees an available order, and taps Accept. The UI looks correct. The API returns success. The feature passes a happy-path test.
Now ask a different set of questions:
What happens if the APK has been modified?
Can another driver submit the same request?
Can a client change an order ID or workflow status?
Does the backend independently verify that this driver is allowed to accept this order?
What evidence proves that the security controls actually work?
These are not questions that can be answered by adding another Android library.
They require security engineering a…
